scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Internet traffic from all internal users became slower and
sometimes flaky. Active TCP connections kept working but new
connections to 203.0.113.x sometimes time out then succeed.
R1 reports it lost an OSPF neighbor. Identify which.

injection.action: kill ospfd on ISPA (primary internet default-originator)

pre_check.command: vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor" | grep -c Full

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: ispa ospfd daemon
Mechanism: Both ISPA and ISPB advertise a default route into
  the OSPF domain via `default-information originate`. R1
  prefers ISPA (lower cost). When ISPA's ospfd dies, R1
  ages out the default learned from ISPA and falls back to
  ISPB's default. During the timeout + reconvergence window,
  new connections fail. Once converged on ISPB, service
  resumes but takes a slightly different path.
Localization: ispa
Root cause: ospfd not running on ispa
Fix: `/etc/init.d/frr restart` on ispa

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): ospfd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router ospf` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists ospfd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the ospf configuration is missing/empty on ispa" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault is in ISPB's OSPF configuration: `passive-interface eth0` has been applied to the interface connecting ISPB to R1 (the CD_ISPB_R1 segment, 203.0.113.4/30). This suppresses all OSPF hello packets on that interface, making it impossible for ISPB to form an OSPF adjacency with R1. The misconfiguration is confirmed by the inline comment `! Passive Interface to R1 [Source 93]` in ISPB's frr.conf, which marks this as the injected fault line.

ISPB was designed to serve as R1's secondary ISP OSPF peer: it runs ospfd with `ip ospf area 0` on eth0, `redistribute connected`, and `default-information originate` (it holds a valid default route `0.0.0.0/0 via 203.0.113.6`). The intent was for ISPB to inject a backup default route into R1's OSPF area 0 so that internet traffic could fail over to the ISPB path when ISPA experiences issues. With the passive interface active, ISPB's ospfd has zero neighbors and its external LSAs (203.0.113.4/30, 216.239.35.4/32, seven redistributed prefixes) are never propagated.

As a result, R1 has only a single internet default route — a DHCP-learned kernel route `K>* 0.0.0.0/0 via 203.0.113.1 eth2` from ISPA. When ISPA has transient forwarding interruptions (evidenced by the short DHCP lease with valid_lft ~500 s), new TCP connections attempting to reach 203.0.113.x cannot be set up and time out, then succeed once ISPA recovers. Established TCP sessions survive because their kernel flow state and cached neighbor entries tolerate brief disruptions. The internal campus OSPF (R1 ↔ csw1 ↔ csw2 and downstream) is fully healthy with both neighbors Full and stable.

Root cause: `passive-interface eth0` in ISPB's `router ospf` stanza prevents OSPF hello emission on the R1-facing link, permanently eliminating the backup ISP OSPF neighbor relationship.

Corrective fix: Remove `passive-interface eth0` from ISPB's OSPF config, and add `network 203.0.113.4/30 area 0` to R1's `router ospf` stanza (or `ip ospf area 0` on R1's eth3) so both sides participate in OSPF on the ISPB transit segment and the adjacency can form.

per_axis.rationale: The agent blames ISPB for a passive-interface misconfiguration, but the ground truth requires identifying ISPA (ospfd not running) as the affected device.
The agent explicitly identifies OSPF/ospfd as the affected component (mentions ospfd, 'router ospf', passive-interface, and OSPF adjacencies).

The agent clearly explains why ISPB did not perform failover: a passive-interface prevented the OSPF adjacency so ISPB never advertised the backup default, leaving R1 reliant on ISPA and causing the observed outage.
The agent recommends removing passive-interface on ISPB and changing OSPF on R1, which does not match the expected fix of restarting FRR on ispa.

The log contains direct evidence for many of the agent's observations (ISPB has ospfd running with no neighbors; R1's default via ISPA), but the agent's final conclusion blames ISPB while ignoring the clear, logged fact that ISPA's ospfd is not running — a critical contradictory observation. Several claims are grounded, but the causal chain and coverage omit or misattribute the true root cause.
